claim: Social tactile stimulation such as affectionate stroking may elicit endogenous OT release in adult humans.
source: It has, therefore, been suggested that social tactile stimulation such as affectionate stroking may elicit endogenous OT release in adult humans (Chen et al., 2020; Kreuder et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research suggesting this relationship

claim: Magnocellular OT neurons in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus send projections to the forebrain and cortical regions mediating olfactory and somatosensory signaling in the brain.
source: It is well-established that magnocellular OT neurons in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus send projections to the forebrain and cortical regions mediating olfactory and somatosensory signaling in the brain (Burbach et al., 2005; Knobloch et al., 2012; Mitre et al., 2018; Oettl et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research establishing this neuroanatomical pathway

claim: A population of parvocellular OT neurons in the PVN is selective for particular forms of affiliative touch.
source: For tactile stimulation, this signaling may rely on a population of parvocellular OT neurons in the PVN selective for particular forms of affiliative touch (Tang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research on parvocellular OT neurons

claim: OT released into the bloodstream via a PVN-pituitary gland pathway modulates the action of vasculature and smooth muscle.
source: OT released into the bloodstream via a PVN-pituitary gland pathway modulates the action of vasculature and smooth muscle (Qin et al., 2009), notably during processes surrounding reproductive behavior in both sexes, as well as parturition and lactation in females (Filippi et al., 2003; Uvnäs-Moberg, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on peripheral OT effects

claim: OT's broad role in parental nurturance and affiliative behavior may reflect a functional extension of its influence on core reproductive and maternal behaviors.
source: OT's broad role in parental nurturance and affiliative behavior may reflect a functional extension of its influence on these core reproductive and maternal behaviors (Walum and Young, 2018), many of which rely on sensory cues such as touch and olfaction, and can even encompass cross-species interactions (Algoe et al., 2017; Nagasawa et al., 2015; Rehn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and theoretical framework

claim: Intranasal OT (IN-OT) administration has shown varying effects on social outcome measures such as face processing.
source: For example, IN-OT have shown varying effects on social outcome measures such as face processing (Fischer-Shofty et al., 2010; Petrovic et al., 2008; Rimmele et al., 2009), empathy (Domes et al., 2007), romantic relationships and bonding (Ditzen et al., 2009; Kreuder et al., 2017; Scheele et al., 2012; Scheele et al., 2013), and romantic touch (Kreuder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies on IN-OT effects

claim: Neuroimaging studies of IN-OT manipulations indicate that many relevant changes occur at the cortical level.
source: Neuroimaging studies of IN-OT manipulations indicate that many relevant changes occur at the cortical level (Wang et al., 2017; Zink and Meyer-Lindenberg, 2012), suggesting more complex modulatory pathways than is implied by a stimulus-driven model focused on signaling from afferent receptors to subcortical brain regions.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior neuroimaging research

claim: There is uncertainty surrounding the mechanisms of action of IN-OT and its degree of equivalence to endogenous release.
source: There is uncertainty surrounding the mechanisms of action of IN-OT and its degree of equivalence to endogenous release, chiefly regarding the questions of whether the molecule crosses the blood-brain barrier, and how peripheral effects can be disentangled from central effects (Churchland and Winkielman, 2012; Striepens et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017; Zink and Meyer-Lindenberg, 2012, but see McCullough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research discussing these uncertainties

claim: OT modulates cardiovascular responses, playing a key role in regulating the autonomic nervous system.
source: OT modulates cardiovascular responses, playing a key role in regulating the autonomic nervous system (Uvnäs-Moberg, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: OT may modulate stress responses via an interplay with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) mechanisms affecting the hormone cortisol.
source: OT may also modulate stress responses via an interplay with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) mechanisms affecting the hormone cortisol, a key mediator of stress responses.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism

claim: Research in rats has suggested a role for OT in particular tactile-mediated social behaviors.
source: Research in rats has suggested a role in particular tactile-mediated social behaviors (Tang et al., 2020), while research in dogs has suggested a role for endogenous OT in touch during the social reunion with their owners, which may also involve cortisol changes (Rehn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in rats

claim: Research in dogs has suggested a role for endogenous OT in touch during the social reunion with their owners, which may also involve cortisol changes.
source: Research in rats has suggested a role in particular tactile-mediated social behaviors (Tang et al., 2020), while research in dogs has suggested a role for endogenous OT in touch during the social reunion with their owners, which may also involve cortisol changes (Rehn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in dogs

claim: Neuroimaging research on touch and OT has implicated the orbitofrontal cortex during foot massage.
source: In, humans, neuroimaging research on touch and OT has implicated the orbitofrontal cortex during foot massage (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior neuroimaging research

claim: C-tactile (CT) afferents are a specific subtype of afferent nerve fiber found in hair-follicle-containing skin in humans.
source: Social, affective touch has also been associated with a specific subtype of afferent nerve fiber called C-tactile (CT) afferents in humans (C-low-threshold mechanoreceptors or C-LTMRs in rodent models), which are found in hair-follicle-containing skin (Löken et al., 2009; Morrison et al., 2010; Olausson et al., 2002; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on CT afferents

claim: CTs increase firing frequency for caress-like touch stimulation, which has correlated with subjective reports of touch pleasantness on a group level.
source: CTs increase firing frequency for caress-like touch stimulation, which has correlated with subjective reports of touch pleasantness on a group level (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Both OT and CTs have been implicated in affective touch.
source: Because both OT and CTs have been implicated in affective touch, it has been proposed that OT may be involved in CT-related neural mechanisms (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge

claim: It has been proposed that OT may be involved in CT-related neural mechanisms.
source: Because both OT and CTs have been implicated in affective touch, it has been proposed that OT may be involved in CT-related neural mechanisms (Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior proposal

claim: Touch from a male to his female romantic partner enhanced her subsequent OT release for touch from an unfamiliar stranger.
source: Namely, touch from a male to his female romantic partner enhanced her subsequent OT release for touch from an unfamiliar stranger, yet females' OT responses to partner touch were dampened following stranger touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Females' OT responses to partner touch were dampened following stranger touch.
source: Namely, touch from a male to his female romantic partner enhanced her subsequent OT release for touch from an unfamiliar stranger, yet females' OT responses to partner touch were dampened following stranger touch.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Hypothalamus and dorsal raphe activation reflected plasma OT changes during the initial social interaction.
source: Hypothalamus and dorsal raphe activation reflected plasma OT changes during the initial social interaction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: In the subsequent interaction, precuneus and parietal-temporal cortex pathways tracked time- and context-dependent variables in an OT-dependent manner.
source: In the subsequent interaction, precuneus and parietal-temporal cortex pathways tracked time- and context-dependent variables in an OT-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: OT-dependent cortical modulation included a region of the medial prefrontal cortex that also covaried with plasma cortisol.
source: This OT-dependent cortical modulation included a region of the medial prefrontal cortex that also covaried with plasma cortisol, suggesting an influence on stress responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: The covariation of mPFC with both OT and cortisol suggests an influence on stress responses.
source: This OT-dependent cortical modulation included a region of the medial prefrontal cortex that also covaried with plasma cortisol, suggesting an influence on stress responses.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed covariation patterns

claim: Modulation between hormones and the brain during human social interactions can flexibly adapt to features of social context over time.
source: These findings demonstrate that modulation between hormones and the brain during human social interactions can flexibly adapt to features of social context over time.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data

claim: Both female and male participants were satisfied with their relationships.
source: CSI scores indicated that both female and male participants were satisfied with their relationships (females: M=139.8, SD = 17.2, males: M=139.6, SD = 15.2), and the participants' assessments of relationship quality correlated with their partners' (r=0.57, p=0.0003).
evidence: Supported by questionnaire data from the study

claim: The participants' assessments of relationship quality correlated with their partners' assessments.
source: CSI scores indicated that both female and male participants were satisfied with their relationships (females: M=139.8, SD = 17.2, males: M=139.6, SD = 15.2), and the participants' assessments of relationship quality correlated with their partners' (r=0.57, p=0.0003).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of questionnaire data

claim: No participants demonstrated clinically significant symptoms of anxiety.
source: STAI scores indicated that no participants demonstrated clinically significant symptoms of anxiety (females STAI-S M=35.6, SD = 9.7; female STAI-T M=40.3, SD = 9.8; males STAI-S M=31.6, SD = 5.7; males STAI-T: M=36.2, SD = 6.7).
evidence: Supported by questionnaire data from the study

claim: The higher participants' trait anxiety, the lower their assessment of relationship quality.
source: The higher participants' trait anxiety, the lower their assessment of relationship quality, with an inverse correlation between STAI-T and CSI scores (r=–0.40, p=0.01 for the participant, r=–0.39, p=0.01 for partner).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of questionnaire data

claim: Partner touch was rated as more pleasant than stranger touch.
source: For trial-by-trail ratings of touch pleasantness, partner touch was rated as more pleasant than stranger touch (F(1, 33)=30.032, p<0.001) with a main effect of higher ratings for arm (F(1, 33)=11.070, p=0.002, effect size f=0.7, partial η2=0.33 at power (1-β error probability)=0.8, α=0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pleasantness ratings

claim: Touch on the arm was rated as more pleasant than touch on the palm.
source: For trial-by-trail ratings of touch pleasantness, partner touch was rated as more pleasant than stranger touch (F(1, 33)=30.032, p<0.001) with a main effect of higher ratings for arm (F(1, 33)=11.070, p=0.002, effect size f=0.7, partial η2=0.33 at power (1-β error probability)=0.8, α=0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pleasantness ratings

claim: Participants who received stranger touch first had lower ratings for stranger touch on the palm compared to stranger touch on the arm.
source: Participants who received stranger touch first had lower ratings for stranger touch on the palm compared to stranger touch on the arm (t=16, p=0.007, d=1.99), reflected in a significant three-way interaction, indicating influences of both familiarity and order on touch pleasantness ratings for palm (F(1, 33)=4.730, p=0.037).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of pleasantness ratings

claim: The stranger was rated as positively trustworthy, with a mean rating of 3.96 on a visual analog scale from –10 (untrustworthy) to 10 (trustworthy).
source: For post-scanning ratings of trustworthiness and attractiveness, the stranger was rated as positively trustworthy, with a mean rating of 3.96 on a visual analog scale from –10 (untrustworthy) to 10 (trustworthy).
evidence: Supported by post-scanning rating data

claim: Stranger attractiveness was near a neutral midpoint, with a mean rating of 0.95 on a visual analog scale from –10 (unattractive) to 10 (attractive).
source: Stranger attractiveness was near a neutral midpoint, with a mean rating of 0.95 on a visual analog scale from –10 (unattractive) to 10 (attractive).
evidence: Supported by post-scanning rating data

claim: The interaction with the nurse was rated as non-stressful, with a mean rating of 5.28 on a scale of –10 (stressful) to 10 (calming).
source: The interaction with the nurse was rated as non-stressful, with a mean rating of 5.28 on a scale of –10 (stressful) to 10 (calming).
evidence: Supported by post-scanning rating data

claim: OT levels increased when the partner was the interactant in the first encounter.
source: As predicted, OT levels increased when the partner was the interactant in the first encounter (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by plasma OT measurements and shown in Figure 2A

claim: When stranger touch was preceded by partner touch OT levels showed a significant dip and recovery during the second touch session.
source: In addition, when stranger touch was preceded by partner touch OT levels showed a significant dip and recovery during the second touch session.
evidence: Supported by plasma OT measurements

claim: There was a three-way interaction between the factors familiarity, order, and sample timepoint for OT levels.
source: These results were revealed by a three-way interaction between the factors familiarity, order, and sample timepoint (F(3, 183.180)=3.034, p=0.031).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma OT data

claim: A significant increase between the first and middle samples in the functional run during stranger touch in the partner first group only drove the contribution of timepoint to the three-way interaction.
source: A significant increase between the first and middle samples in the functional run during stranger touch in the partner first group only (p=0.027) drove the contribution of timepoint to the three-way interaction.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma OT data

claim: There was a two-way interaction between the factors familiarity and order for OT levels.
source: There was also a two-way interaction between the factors familiarity and order (F(1, 183.169)=11.216, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma OT data

claim: Individuals' mean OT in the initial encounter predicted mean OT levels in the second encounter.
source: Individuals' mean OT in the initial encounter predicted mean OT levels in the second (partner-stranger r=0.97, p<0.001; stranger-partner r=0.57, p=0.03).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma OT data

claim: Mean plasma cortisol levels were higher for stranger than for partner during the first encounter.
source: Here, mean plasma cortisol levels were higher for stranger than for partner during the first encounter (Figure 2D) and these decreased as mean OT levels increased during the course of the experiment.
evidence: Supported by plasma cortisol measurements and shown in Figure 2D

claim: Plasma cortisol levels decreased as mean OT levels increased during the course of the experiment.
source: Here, mean plasma cortisol levels were higher for stranger than for partner during the first encounter (Figure 2D) and these decreased as mean OT levels increased during the course of the experiment.
evidence: Supported by plasma hormone measurements

claim: Familiarity and order interacted in plasma cortisol levels.
source: Cortisol showed a significant influence on partner or stranger (familiarity) but also their presentation order (interaction, F(1, 130)=54.89, p<0.001; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma cortisol data

claim: Cortisol levels were higher when the stranger was presented first, compared to when he was presented second.
source: Cortisol levels were higher when the stranger was presented first, compared to when he was presented second (p=0.008).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma cortisol data

claim: Stranger touch elicited a greater cortisol increase compared to partner touch.
source: In addition, stranger or partner (familiarity) as well as time point significantly influenced the participant's cortisol levels (F(1, 130)=15.67, p<0.001 and F(2, 130)=3.16, p=0.045, respectively). Cortisol levels were higher at the beginning of the touch session compared to the end (p=0.039) and stranger touch elicited a greater cortisol increase compared to partner touch (p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma cortisol data

claim: Cortisol levels were higher at the beginning of the touch session compared to the end.
source: In addition, stranger or partner (familiarity) as well as time point significantly influenced the participant's cortisol levels (F(1, 130)=15.67, p<0.001 and F(2, 130)=3.16, p=0.045, respectively). Cortisol levels were higher at the beginning of the touch session compared to the end (p=0.039) and stranger touch elicited a greater cortisol increase compared to partner touch (p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma cortisol data

claim: Cortisol showed higher overall levels than OT.
source: Cortisol showed higher overall levels than OT (a main effect of hormone, F(1, 180.593)=68.574, p<0.001; OT M ± SEM: partner first: 67.781±6.019, stranger first: 42.959±1.816, p=0.017; cortisol M ± SEM: partner first: 80.346±5.486, stranger first: 101.633±6.306, p=0.040).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma hormone data

claim: OT levels were higher but cortisol levels were lower in the partner first condition as compared to stranger first.
source: In addition, OT levels were higher but cortisol levels were lower in the partner first condition as compared to stranger first (F(1,180.593)=28,751, p<0.001), and a statistical interaction indicated a mutual influence between familiarity and order (F(1, 178.355)=10.565, p=0.001; also found in the two previous individual models; Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of plasma hormone data and shown in Figure 2F

claim: Familiarity, order, and OT showed mutual influences in cortical clusters including the right superior occipital gyrus extending into the right cuneus, and the left angular gyrus.
source: This 3dLME analysis revealed cortical clusters in which familiarity, order, and OT showed mutual influences (a three-way interaction; Table 1). These clusters included the right superior occipital gyrus (SOG) extending into the right cuneus, and the left angular gyrus (AG).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: BOLD increase in SOG/cuneus showed a positive relationship with OT change in the partner first group.
source: Specifically, whereas BOLD increase in SOG/cuneus showed a positive relationship in the partner first group (partner first, stranger second), these relationships were negative in the stranger first group, particularly for stranger.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: BOLD increase in AG showed positive or flat relationships with OT change in all conditions except for partner second in the stranger first group, which was negative.
source: BOLD increase in AG showed positive or flat relationships with OT change in all conditions except for partner second in the stranger first group, which was negative (the higher the BOLD, the lower the OT change).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Familiarity and OT interacted in the bilateral angular gyrus (SMG/AG), inferior temporal gyrus (ITG), middle temporal gyrus (MTG), right temporal pole (TP), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: Familiarity and OT interacted in the bilateral angular gyrus (SMG/AG), inferior temporal gyrus (ITG), middle temporal gyrus (MTG), right temporal pole (TP), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC, on the mid-orbital gyrus), among other regions (Figure 2C; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 2C and Table 1

claim: For parietotemporal and medial prefrontal regions, individuals showing greater OT increase during the functional run were also more likely to show higher BOLD during partner compared to stranger touch.
source: For all these areas, individuals showing greater OT increase during the functional run were also more likely to show higher BOLD during partner compared to stranger touch, reflecting a more positive relationship between BOLD signal and OT change for partner (the higher the BOLD, the greater the degree of OT change).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: A right hemisphere cluster encompassing inferior and middle temporal gyri (ITG and MTG) showed a main effect of OT covariate.
source: A right hemisphere cluster encompassing inferior and middle temporal gyri (ITG and MTG) also showed a main effect of OT covariate (a positive relationship between BOLD and OT change; Table 1) as well as an interaction between order and OT (Table 1; see also Figure 4A), reflecting a more positive relationship between BOLD signal and degree of OT increase in the stranger first group.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: BOLD was overall greater for stranger than partner in bilateral middle frontal gyrus (MFG) and right AG, regardless of the degree of OT change.
source: Regardless of the degree of OT change, BOLD was overall greater for stranger than partner (a main effect of familiarity) in bilateral middle frontal gyrus (MFG) and right AG, among other regions (Table 1), reflecting generally higher means but a narrower range of variability for stranger than partner.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: BOLD was greater for the palm than the arm in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG) and bilateral precentral gyrus (PrCG).
source: BOLD was greater for the palm than the arm (a main effect of the stimulation site; Table 1) in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG) and bilateral precentral gyrus (PrCG).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: No statistical interactions were observed between the site of stimulation and OT covariate.
source: No statistical interactions were observed between the site of stimulation and OT covariate.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Raphe nuclei and hypothalamus showed a greater positive covariation between BOLD and OT change for partner touch compared to stranger touch in the first run.
source: Raphe nuclei (whole brain) and hypothalamus (ROI analysis) showed a greater positive covariation between BOLD and OT change for partner touch compared to stranger touch in the first run (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Within the hypothalamus cluster, a subset of 15 voxels showing greater increases for partner touch than stranger touch survived stricter cluster correction at p=0.002.
source: Within this cluster, a subset of 15 voxels showing greater increases for partner touch than stranger touch survived stricter cluster correction at p=0.002.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis with small volume correction

claim: OT-BOLD covariance in the hypothalamus and dorsal Raphe showed a greater negative correlation for stranger touch during the initial encounter.
source: OT-BOLD covariance in the hypothalamus and dorsal Raphe showed a greater negative correlation for stranger touch during the initial encounter (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3

claim: All standardized residuals for the hypothalamus region-of-interest fell within ±3 standard deviations from the trendline.
source: These showed that all standardized residuals fell within ±3.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of residuals

claim: The regressions were significant at p<0.05, for both hypothalamus and Raphe nuclei.
source: The regressions were significant at p<0.05, for both hypothalamus (p=0.003 for partner first, p=0.03 for stranger first) and Raphe nuclei.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: In parietotemporal clusters, the higher an individual's BOLD, the higher her OT levels when receiving partner touch in the second run, as compared to those receiving stranger touch in the second run.
source: In parietotemporal clusters, the higher an individual's BOLD, the higher her OT levels when receiving partner touch in the second run, as compared to those receiving stranger touch in the second run (in whom this OT-BOLD covariation was less positive).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Parietotemporal clusters showing OT-BOLD covariation in the second run included right AG, right TP, and right superior temporal gyrus (STG).
source: These parietotemporal clusters were also seen in the interaction maps in which OT interacted with familiarity (right AG, right TP; Figure 2C) and order (right MTG). Additional clusters were revealed in the right superior temporal gyrus (STG), among other activations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: There was no activation difference between partner and stranger touch in the partner first group when comparing partner first vs. stranger second.
source: There was no activation difference between partner and stranger touch in the partner first group.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: There was no activation difference between partner and stranger touch in the stranger first group when comparing stranger first vs. partner second.
source: There was no activation difference between partner and stranger touch in the stranger first group.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Linear mixed model of factors order and familiarity with cortisol covariate did not show any significant main effect or interaction.
source: As in the OT analysis, we searched for brain correlates of touch interactions as influenced by familiarity (partner, stranger), order (partner first, stranger first), and cortisol plasma level, performing a linear mixed-effects modeling analysis (3dLME in AFNI; n=26). Again, we adopted the model with random intercept and random slope, and cortisol mean values (percent change from baseline) for each participant were centered around the mean of each of the four conditions (partner first, stranger first, partner second, stranger second) prior to the analysis. Results did not show any significant main effect or interaction.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: In the first run, the two groups did not differ in terms of activation according to the identity of the stroker when using cortisol as a covariate.
source: In the first run, the two groups did not differ in terms of activation according to the identity of the stroker.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: In the second run, there was no differential activation between partner first and stranger first groups related to the identity of the stroker when using cortisol as a covariate.
source: In the second run, there was no differential activation between partner first and stranger first groups related to the identity of the stroker.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: For participants who had partner touch first, partner compared to stranger touch covaried with cortisol in the left ACC, right SMG, bilateral ventromedial prefrontal cortex, bilateral calcarine gyrus, right lingual gyrus, left TP, and left PO.
source: For participants who had partner touch first, partner compared to stranger touch covaried with cortisol in the left ACC, right SMG, bilateral ventromedial prefrontal cortex, bilateral calcarine gyrus, right lingual gyrus, left TP, and left PO (all at p=0.002).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Regions showing cortisol covariation for partner vs. stranger in the partner first group showed a more negative relationship between BOLD and cortisol for partner.
source: These regions showed a more negative relationship between BOLD and cortisol for partner (individuals with higher BOLD had higher cortisol).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: When comparing brain activity in the two runs in the group of participants who had stranger touch first, there were no cortisol-related differences in brain activity between partner and stranger touch.
source: When comparing brain activity in the two runs in the group of participants who had stranger touch first, we found no cortisol-related differences in brain activity between partner and stranger touch.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Brain areas showing significant interactions between familiarity and order at both 2 and 2.5 min time lags included bilateral precuneus, right SMG, left inferior parietal lobule, right posterior cingulate cortex, right postcentral gyrus, and right parietal operculum.
source: This analysis revealed brain areas showing significant interactions between familiarity and order at both 2 and 2.5 min, with higher BOLD during stranger first than partner first, but no difference between stranger second and partner second (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 3). No activations were observed for the remaining time lags. 2 min. Bilateral precuneus, right SMG, left inferior parietal lobule, right posterior cingulate cortex, right postcentral gyrus, and right parietal operculum showed increased BOLD corresponding to the pattern of changes in OT levels observed 2 min after the activation (p=0.002; Figure 4B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis using custom OT regressor

claim: Two and half minutes before observed changes in OT levels, increased BOLD in the bilateral precuneus and right paracentral lobule corresponded with the temporal pattern of OT changes.
source: 2.5 min. Two and half minutes before observed changes in OT levels, increased BOLD in the bilateral precuneus and right paracentral lobule corresponded with the temporal pattern of OT changes (all at p=0.002, Figure 4B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis using custom OT regressor

claim: In the partner first group, a cluster in ITG was revealed that overlapped with the ITG/TP clusters in which OT interacted with familiarity and order.
source: In the partner first group, a cluster in ITG was revealed, which overlapped with the ITG/TP clusters in which OT interacted with familiarity and order, respectively (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis with pleasantness covariate

claim: In the ITG cluster, individuals that showed higher BOLD activation for partner compared to stranger also showed the largest difference in pleasantness ratings between partner and stranger touch.
source: Here, individuals that showed higher BOLD activation for partner compared to stranger also showed the largest difference in ratings between partner and stranger touch.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis with pleasantness covariate

claim: When the stranger delivered touch in the second encounter, ITG activation increased with touch pleasantness during the run.
source: When the stranger delivered touch in the second encounter, ITG activation increased with touch pleasantness during the run (r=0.65, p=0.003; Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis with pleasantness covariate

claim: Brain areas showing increased activity irrespective of condition were: bilateral supramarginal gyrus (SMG), bilateral postcentral gyrus, left precentral gyrus, left superior parietal lobule (SPL), left parietal operculum (PO), bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), bilateral anterior insula, right cerebellum, right supplementary motor area (SMA), and right amygdala.
source: Brain areas showing increased activity irrespective of condition were: bilateral supramarginal gyrus (SMG), bilateral postcentral gyrus, left precentral gyrus, left superior parietal lobule (SPL), left parietal operculum (PO), bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), bilateral anterior insula, right cerebellum, right supplementary motor area (SMA), and right amygdala.
evidence: Supported by conjunction analysis of fMRI data

claim: There was a common deactivation in the right precentral gyrus across all touch conditions.
source: There was a common deactivation in the right precentral gyrus.
evidence: Supported by conjunction analysis of fMRI data

claim: BOLD signal change in the left amygdala was sensitive to partner-stranger differences, greater for the stranger in the first encounter.
source: While BOLD signal change in the left amygdala was high across conditions, it was also sensitive to partner-stranger differences (main effect of familiarity, F(1,16) = 5.8, p=0.02), greater for the stranger in the first encounter.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: Touch-mediated social interactions in human females elicited endogenous OT and brain responses in a covariant manner.
source: The most general finding was that touch-mediated social interactions in human females elicited endogenous OT and brain responses in a covariant manner.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data

claim: OT and neural changes were modulated by the familiarity of the person delivering touch, as well as the recent history of social interaction.
source: Beyond this, OT and neural changes were modulated by the familiarity of the person delivering touch, as well as the recent history of social interaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data

claim: The effect of contextual factors on within-subject endogenous OT changes manifested in a mutual influence between the familiarity of the social interactant and the order of his presentation over two immediately successive social interactions.
source: The effect of these contextual factors on within-subject endogenous OT changes manifested in a mutual influence between the familiarity of the social interactant (partner or stranger) and the order of his presentation over two immediately successive social interactions (partner then stranger, or stranger then partner).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data

claim: The influence of familiarity and order on OT was driven by a greater increase in plasma OT responses for the stranger following partner touch, in the absence of a corresponding increase for partner touch following stranger touch.
source: This influence was driven by a greater increase in plasma OT responses for the stranger following partner touch, in the absence of a corresponding increase for partner touch following stranger touch (Figure 2A).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The dependence of OT responses on both familiarity and presentation order is consistent with evidence for cumulative effects of central OT exposure over repeated interactions with specific individuals.
source: This dependence of OT responses on both familiarity and presentation order is consistent with evidence for cumulative effects of central OT exposure over repeated interactions with specific individuals (Burkett et al., 2016), as well as the established context-sensitivity of OT effects in nonhuman mammals (Bartz et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior research

claim: The initial partner encounter may have introduced a bias for OT increase during the subsequent stranger encounter.
source: A tentative interpretation of this pattern is that the initial partner encounter may have introduced a bias for OT increase during the subsequent stranger encounter, though not as a sustained carryover from the preceding partner interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed OT pattern

claim: The recovery of OT in the stranger-second condition could reflect a facilitation of underlying endogenous release mechanisms following the prior partner interaction.
source: The recovery of OT in the stranger-second condition could thus reflect a facilitation of underlying endogenous release mechanisms following the prior partner interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed OT pattern

claim: Endogenous OT changes may reflect mechanisms that selectively bias the way social stimuli are processed in the central nervous system during social interactions, with high dependence on contextual information.
source: Overall, these endogenous OT changes may reflect mechanisms that selectively bias the way social stimuli are processed in the central nervous system during social interactions, with high dependence on contextual information.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data

claim: Co-modulation between OT changes and BOLD in parietotemporal pathways may reflect updating of contextual information.
source: Co-modulation between OT changes and BOLD in parietotemporal pathways may reflect updating of contextual information, possibly enhancing the salience of incoming sensory signals (Johnson et al., 2017; Shamay-Tsoory and Abu-Akel, 2016; Sripada et al., 2013) or of personally-relevant stimuli Alaerts et al., 2021 following the initial encounter.
evidence: Speculative interpretation with reference to prior research

claim: OT-brain co-modulation may find and maintain a stable response profile following partner touch, even after an unfamiliar stranger is presented.
source: A speculative interpretation is that OT-brain co-modulation may find and maintain a stable response profile following partner touch, even after an unfamiliar stranger is presented, whereas such recalibration can be more sluggish following an initial encounter with the stranger.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed patterns

claim: OT-brain co-modulation may involve an enlistment of parietotemporal regions in gain control mechanisms.
source: This may reflect an enlistment of parietotemporal regions in gain control mechanisms (Grinevich and Ludwig, 2021)—more akin to a dimmer switch than an on-off button— with the 'dimmer' tuning from a wider, more flexible response range under higher contextual certainty (partner first) to a narrower, less flexible range under lower contextual certainty (stranger first).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with reference to prior research

claim: The preferential increase in plasma OT levels for the partner in the initial touch encounter is consistent with the familiarity-dependent effects of OT in rodents.
source: In the initial touch encounter, the preferential increase in plasma OT levels for the partner is consistent with the familiarity-dependent effects of OT in rodents (Burkett et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior research

claim: The partner-stranger difference in OT was reflected in hypothalamus OT-covariance as a function of individual changes in plasma OT levels.
source: This basic partner-stranger difference was reflected in hypothalamus OT-covariance as a function of individual changes in plasma OT levels (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The hypothalamus OT-covariance finding is in accord with the conserved mammalian neuroanatomy of central OT release, in which hypothalamic nuclei, particularly the PVN, synthesize OT and stimulate its release in the brain.
source: This is in accord with the conserved mammalian neuroanatomy of central OT release, in which hypothalamic nuclei, particularly the PVN, synthesize OT and stimulate its release in the brain (Burbach et al., 2005; Knobloch et al., 2012; Mitre et al., 2018; Oettl et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to established knowledge

claim: In rats, stroking touch increases Fos protein expression in PVN.
source: In rats, stroking touch increases Fos protein expression in PVN (Okabe et al., 2015), and recent evidence from freely-interacting female rats indicates that a population of parvocellular OT neurons in PVN is selectively tuned to social touch stimulation (Tang et al., 2020) and also that this is associated with subsequent changes in levels of plasma OT (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in rats

claim: Recent evidence from freely-interacting female rats indicates that a population of parvocellular OT neurons in PVN is selectively tuned to social touch stimulation and this is associated with subsequent changes in levels of plasma OT.
source: In rats, stroking touch increases Fos protein expression in PVN (Okabe et al., 2015), and recent evidence from freely-interacting female rats indicates that a population of parvocellular OT neurons in PVN is selectively tuned to social touch stimulation (Tang et al., 2020) and also that this is associated with subsequent changes in levels of plasma OT (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research in rats

claim: When the stranger touched first, BOLD in both the hypothalamus and dorsal Raphe was greater the lower the mean OT across individuals.
source: Specifically, when the stranger touched first, BOLD in both the hypothalamus and dorsal Raphe was greater the lower the mean OT across individuals (Figures 1 and 3), whereas no such modulation of OT-BOLD covariance was observed for partner.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figures 1 and 3

claim: The negative relationship between BOLD and OT during stranger touch may reflect descending modulatory influence on afferent touch signals from the periphery.
source: This may reflect descending modulatory influence on afferent touch signals from the periphery, manifesting here as a negative relationship between BOLD and OT during stranger touch (the BOLD signal cannot distinguish hemodynamic activity resulting from excitation or inhibition).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern

claim: Central effects of IN-OT have consistently been found ~45 min post-administration.
source: Central effects of IN-OT have consistently been found ~45 min post-administration (Martins et al., 2020; Sripada et al., 2013; Valstad et al., 2017), but there is less direct evidence about the timecourse of central endogenous OT release into the periphery in humans.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The pattern-covariant engagement of the precuneus at 2.5 min preceding sampling, and of precuneus, retrosplenial cortex, and mPFC at 2 min, is within the frame of the half-life of OT in the blood.
source: The pattern-covariant engagement of the precuneus at 2.5 min preceding sampling, and of precuneus, retrosplenial cortex, and mPFC at 2 min, is within the frame of the half-life of OT in the blood (Pow and Morris, 1989) and may reflect events surrounding central OT release (Qin et al., 2009; Figure 4B).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior research on OT half-life

claim: It is possible that any descending OT influence from the brain to the periphery instates a 'reafferent loop' in which central-to-peripheral changes can, in turn, influence incoming sensory information.
source: Although the present results lack the sufficient temporal and causal resolution to address this, it is possible that any descending OT influence from the brain to the periphery instates a 'reafferent loop' in which central-to-peripheral changes can, in turn, influence incoming sensory information, perhaps at the level of spinal and/or brainstem mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative interpretation acknowledging limitations

claim: Retrosplenial cortex projects to mPFC.
source: Retrosplenial cortex projects to mPFC (Margulies et al., 2009), while precuneus is functionally connected to the AG region showing interactions between OT and familiarity (Figure 2C; bilateral AG extending to left SMG) and OT and order (right AG), described above.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Precuneus is functionally connected to the AG region showing interactions between OT and familiarity and OT and order.
source: Retrosplenial cortex projects to mPFC (Margulies et al., 2009), while precuneus is functionally connected to the AG region showing interactions between OT and familiarity (Figure 2C; bilateral AG extending to left SMG) and OT and order (right AG), described above.
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to established knowledge

claim: IN-OT administration can induce changes in functional connectivity between precuneus and AG.
source: IN-OT administration can also induce changes in functional connectivity between precuneus and AG (Kumar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The precuneus, retrosplenial cortex, and mPFC may act as arbiters of activation in parietotemporal and limbic networks, potentially influencing responses to social touch via contextual integration and affecting regulation processes.
source: These findings imply that the precuneus, retrosplenial cortex, and mPFC may act as arbiters of activation in parietotemporal and limbic networks, potentially influencing responses to social touch via contextual integration and affecting regulation processes.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data

claim: The covariant relationship of ITG activation with plasma OT changes as well as touch pleasantness ratings suggests a potential role for this region in maintaining receptivity to touch following contextual shifts.
source: For example, the covariant relationship of ITG activation with plasma OT changes as well as touch pleasantness ratings (Figure 4A), suggests a potential role for this region in maintaining receptivity to touch following contextual shifts.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: OT-dependent neural dynamics may play a critical role in calibrating social receptivity, especially over multiple social encounters.
source: Such OT-dependent neural dynamics may play a critical role in calibrating social receptivity, especially over multiple social encounters.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data

claim: OT has been implicated in stress regulation via corticotropin-releasing-hormone (CRH) pathways that result in cortisol changes, and so may act as a physiological regulator of acute stress-related responses.
source: OT has been implicated in stress regulation via corticotropin-releasing-hormone (CRH) pathways that result in cortisol changes, and so may act as a physiological regulator of acute stress-related responses (Ditzen et al., 2009; Grewen et al., 2005; Petersson and Uvnäs-Moberg, 2003; Vargas-Martínez et al., 2014; Winter and Jurek, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Plasma cortisol levels covaried with BOLD for partner in the initial encounter in several regions, including a mPFC activation that contained an OT-sensitive cluster.
source: Here, plasma cortisol levels covaried with BOLD for partner in the initial encounter in several regions, including a mPFC activation that contained an OT-sensitive cluster (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Activation in mPFC and superior temporal gyrus (STG) decreased for initial stranger touch as a function of cortisol, compared to partner.
source: Further, activation in both mPFC, implicated in cortical-amygdala signaling following IN-OT, and superior temporal gyrus (STG), implicated across a range of multisensory integration, including touch (Davidovic et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2016; Voos et al., 2013), decreased for initial stranger touch as a function of cortisol, compared to partner.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: These selective hormone-brain changes support the view that endogenous OT's role in human social interaction is heavily modulated by contextual factors.
source: Taken together, these selective hormone-brain changes support the view that endogenous OT's role in human social interaction is heavily modulated by contextual factors (Bartz et al., 2011), and provides further evidence that this role can involve modulation in a positive or a negative direction, depending on the situation (Hovey et al., 2016; LoParo et al., 2016; Rickenbacher et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior research

claim: Endogenous OT's role can involve modulation in a positive or a negative direction, depending on the situation.
source: Taken together, these selective hormone-brain changes support the view that endogenous OT's role in human social interaction is heavily modulated by contextual factors (Bartz et al., 2011), and provides further evidence that this role can involve modulation in a positive or a negative direction, depending on the situation (Hovey et al., 2016; LoParo et al., 2016; Rickenbacher et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior research

claim: In prairie voles, higher levels of endogenous OT can mediate prosocial grooming of stressed others.
source: For example, in prairie voles, higher levels of endogenous OT can mediate prosocial grooming of stressed others (Burkett et al., 2016), but optogenetic manipulation of the same PVN OT neurons in freely-behaving mice can result in either prosocial or antagonistic behavior (Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Optogenetic manipulation of PVN OT neurons in freely-behaving mice can result in either prosocial or antagonistic behavior.
source: For example, in prairie voles, higher levels of endogenous OT can mediate prosocial grooming of stressed others (Burkett et al., 2016), but optogenetic manipulation of the same PVN OT neurons in freely-behaving mice can result in either prosocial or antagonistic behavior (Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: OT and OT receptor genotypes have been shown to play a role in antagonistic social behaviors such as the defense of offspring in rats and aggression in rodents and humans.
source: OT and OT receptor genotypes have also been shown to play a role in antagonistic social behaviors such as the defense of offspring in rats (Rickenbacher et al., 2017) and aggression in rodents and humans (Hovey et al., 2016; LoParo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The bilateral amygdalae were activated in a general fashion across all touch encounters.
source: The bilateral amygdalae were activated in a general fashion across all encounters (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5), with the left amygdala selective for stranger touch, particularly in the first encounter (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Amygdala activation has been widely implicated in human IN-OT studies, yet with inconsistent reports of the direction of BOLD changes.
source: Amygdala activation has been widely implicated in human IN-OT studies (Kirsch et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2019; Motoki et al., 2016; Sripada et al., 2013), yet with inconsistent reports of the direction of BOLD changes, implying a dependence on experimental and methodological factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: In mice, OT receptor-expressing neurons in the medial amygdala have been found to mediate olfactory-based social familiarity effects.
source: In mice, OT receptor-expressing neurons in the medial amygdala have been found to mediate olfactory-based social familiarity effects (Ferguson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The general activation of the amygdala by stranger touch supports the proposal that its prominent role in human and nonhuman primate OT studies may be indirect.
source: Here, though, stranger touch activated the amygdala in a general fashion (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5), supporting the proposal that its prominent role in human and nonhuman primate OT studies may be indirect (Eckstein et al., 2017; Gothard and Fuglevand, 2022; Putnam et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference drawn from the data in relation to prior proposals

claim: IN-OT has been observed to increase the pleasantness of touch.
source: IN-OT has been observed to increase the pleasantness of touch (Chen et al., 2020), and individuals with higher salivary OT levels have reported greater touch pleasantness (Portnova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Individuals with higher salivary OT levels have reported greater touch pleasantness.
source: IN-OT has been observed to increase the pleasantness of touch (Chen et al., 2020), and individuals with higher salivary OT levels have reported greater touch pleasantness (Portnova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CT afferent nerve responses in the skin have been associated with subjective touch pleasantness of caress-like stimuli on a group level.
source: Likewise, CT afferent nerve responses in the skin have been associated with subjective touch pleasantness of caress-like stimuli on a group level (Löken et al., 2009), though pleasantness ratings for touch show individual variability and lack of specificity (Croy et al., 2021; Sailer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Pleasantness ratings for touch show individual variability and lack of specificity.
source: Likewise, CT afferent nerve responses in the skin have been associated with subjective touch pleasantness of caress-like stimuli on a group level (Löken et al., 2009), though pleasantness ratings for touch show individual variability and lack of specificity (Croy et al., 2021; Sailer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: This experiment provided no supporting evidence for a putative relationship between OT and CT afferent nerve activity associated with affective touch.
source: However, this experiment provided no supporting evidence for a putative relationship between OT and CT afferent nerve activity associated with affective touch.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data

claim: Primary somatosensory cortex showed selective activation for touch on the palm.
source: Primary somatosensory cortex showed selective activation for touch on the palm.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: No OT-BOLD covariance was observed in primary somatosensory cortex or in arm-specific regions such as the posterior insula/PO.
source: Yet no OT-BOLD covariance was observed here or in arm-specific regions such as the posterior insula/PO, which might have indicated a link between stimulation of CT-rich skin and endogenous OT.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis

claim: In rodent models, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) expression has so far not been identified in dorsal horn neurons of the spinothalamic tract projecting to the specific thalamic pathways putatively shared by CT afferents.
source: In rodent models, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) expression has so far not been identified in dorsal horn neurons of the spinothalamic tract projecting to the specific thalamic pathways putatively shared by CT afferents (Gauriau and Bernard, 2004; Moreno-López et al., 2013; Nersesyan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Participants found palm touch from a stranger less pleasant during the initial encounter.
source: On a subjective level, participants found palm touch from a stranger less pleasant during the initial encounter, which was not predicted.
evidence: Supported by pleasantness rating data

claim: The finding that palm touch from a stranger was less pleasant may reflect a functional difference in the palm's prominent role in active sensorimotor exploration.
source: This potentially reflects a functional difference in the palm's prominent role in active sensorimotor exploration (Morrison, 2022), and perhaps potentiation of approach or withdrawal from others' touch.
evidence: Speculative interpretation with reference to prior research

claim: Different methods for detecting plasma OT have yielded different and sometimes uncorrelated sets of value ranges.
source: Different methods for detecting plasma OT have yielded different and sometimes uncorrelated sets of value ranges, with measurement issues centering around the selectivity with which testing components detect bound or unbound protein, or whole or fragmentary molecules.
evidence: Established knowledge about OT measurement issues

claim: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has consistently been found to correlate more strongly with brain OT levels than does plasma OT.
source: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has consistently been found to correlate more strongly with brain OT levels than does plasma OT, while CSF and plasma OT measurements have shown weak or no correlation (Caicedo Mera et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CSF and plasma OT measurements have shown weak or no correlation.
source: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) has consistently been found to correlate more strongly with brain OT levels than does plasma OT, while CSF and plasma OT measurements have shown weak or no correlation (Caicedo Mera et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: At least a proportion of inconsistencies in reported findings may depend on a historical tendency to investigate basal levels, rather than acute stimuli more likely to evoke coordinated, biologically-meaningful responses across the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: However, at least a proportion of inconsistencies in reported findings may depend on a historical tendency to investigate basal levels, rather than acute stimuli more likely to evoke coordinated, biologically-meaningful responses across the central and peripheral nervous systems.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of methodological issues in the field

claim: Within-subject serial sampling allowed assessment of evoked OT changes with respect to individual baselines.
source: In this study, though, within-subject serial sampling allowed assessment of evoked OT changes with respect to individual baselines.
evidence: Description of the study's methodological approach

claim: The covariation of OT changes and their temporal patterns with BOLD points to a relationship between the central and peripheral effects of ecologically-evoked endogenous OT, but cannot directly demonstrate it.
source: The covariation of these changes and their temporal patterns with BOLD points to a relationship between the central and peripheral effects of ecologically-evoked endogenous OT, but cannot directly demonstrate it.

source: Most human studies manipulating OT (usually via nasal administration) have been performed in male populations.

claim: Recent research in rodents has focused on OT-touch mechanisms in female samples.
source: In contrast, the present study used a 'female-first' strategy which moves to redress this imbalance Shansky and Murphy, 2021; likewise, recent research in rodents has focused on OT-touch mechanisms in female samples (Tang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: In this study, there was no effect of the cycle phase on evoked OT changes.
source: Here, we found no effect of the cycle phase on evoked OT changes.

claim: An important question for future research is whether, and to what extent, these results in human females generalize to males.
source: An important question for future research is whether, and to what extent, these results in human females generalize to males, especially with regard to any familiarity-dependent bias in endogenous OT.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions

claim: A positive social interaction context (such as a pleasant touch interaction with one's partner) may selectively bias the system towards a certain shorter-term neurohormonal response profile.
source: A positive social interaction context (such as a pleasant touch interaction with one's partner) may selectively bias the system towards a certain shorter-term neurohormonal response profile, whereas a less certain or less positive social context (such as an unusual interaction with a stranger) may bias it towards a different profile.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data

claim: Starting the day with a positive social interaction can set up a virtuous circle that perpetuates itself through the day's social interactions.
source: For example, this could mean that starting the day with a positive social interaction can set up a virtuous circle that perpetuates itself through the day's social interactions; whereas an uncertain or negative interaction could bias one's responses towards remaining dampened.

source: Such differential outcomes may potentially influence neural processing and behavior in longer-term social interactions.

source: An important avenue for future research will be to investigate the behavioral effects of these neural and physiological differences, especially with respect to social relationships over time.

claim: Touch-mediated social interactions evoked changes in endogenous OT, indicating the importance of the stimulus.
source: Touch-mediated social interactions evoked changes in endogenous OT, indicating the importance of the stimulus.

claim: OT responses were influenced by specific features of social context, with the plasma of OT levels showing biases depending on the familiarity of the interacting person and the recent history of interaction.

claim: Adaptive OT responses could reflect a gain-control-like role for OT-brain neuromodulation, comparable to a dimmer switch.
source: Such adaptive responses could reflect a gain-control-like role for OT-brain neuromodulation, comparable to a dimmer switch, which can effectively preserve stability with respect to established social relationships while also allowing for a change in new ones (possibly via increases or decreases in inhibitory influence).

source: 42 females in committed heterosexual romantic relationships of at least one year (age M=24.6 years, SD = 4.6, Supplementary file 6), participated in the study with their male partners (age M=26.8 years, SD = 6.0).

claim: Female participants were included if they were between 19–40 years, were not pregnant or breastfeeding, did not use estrogen-based contraceptives, and were not undergoing current or recent hormone therapy.

claim: The mean OT of cycling participants fell within one standard deviation of noncycling participants for both partner and stranger.
source: The mean OT of cycling participants fell within one standard deviation of noncycling participants for both partner and stranger (noncycling: 68.8 pg/ml±43.4 pg/ml for partner, 64.1±40.3 pg/ml for stranger; cycling: 62.9 pg/ml±31.1 pg/ml for partner, 48.6±21.3 pg/ml for stranger), indicating that cycle did not affect the variability of mean plasma OT.

claim: Cycle did not affect the variability of mean plasma OT.
source: The mean OT of cycling participants fell within one standard deviation of noncycling participants for both partner and stranger (noncycling: 68.8 pg/ml±43.4 pg/ml for partner, 64.1±40.3 pg/ml for stranger; cycling: 62.9 pg/ml±31.1 pg/ml for partner, 48.6±21.3 pg/ml for stranger), indicating that cycle did not affect the variability of mean plasma OT.
